memoryText: For to us a child is born, to us a son is given; and the government shall be upon his shoulder, and his name shall be called Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace.
readingInstruction: No new reading today. Read Isaiah 9:6 slowly, several times, and then say it from memory. Read the meditation and the week in review, and choose one of the three questions to write about, pray over, or share with someone.
memoryVerseMeditation:
This verse is among the best loved in the Bible, and it is easy to hear it as only a Christmas carol. Read it today as Isaiah’s first hearers did, in a time of fear and darkness.

“For to us a child is born.” The Messiah will be truly human, born into the world as every child is. “To us a son is given.” He is a gift. The first phrase says what he is, a real child. The second says where he comes from, a gift from God. He is both fully one of us and given to us from above.

“The government shall be upon his shoulder.” A child with the weight of the world’s government on his shoulder. In the ancient world, the key or the robe of office was worn on the shoulder. The one who rules is the child. It is a paradox that the New Testament unfolds, a king born in a manger, who rules from a cross.

Then four names. “Wonderful Counselor” means that he has wisdom beyond ours, and that he never gives bad advice. “Mighty God” means that he is not merely human. He is God, the divine warrior. “Everlasting Father” means that he cares for his people with a father’s love and does so forever. “Prince of Peace” means that he is the source of wholeness, and the reconciler between God and man.

Say the names slowly. Choose one that you most need today. If you are confused, he is your Counselor. If you are afraid, he is the Mighty God. If you feel alone, he is the Everlasting Father. If you are anxious or divided, he is your Prince of Peace.
weekInReview: This week you read the oracles of Isaiah’s first section. You read the great promises of the Messiah: the light in Galilee, the child born to us, the shoot from Jesse’s stump, and the kingdom where the earth is filled with the knowledge of the LORD. You took a doctrinal pause on the holiness of God, linking Isaiah’s vision to Peter’s call to be holy. You surveyed the oracles against Babylon, Philistia, Moab, Egypt, Jerusalem, and Tyre, and saw that God rules all the nations and even promises to bless Egypt and Assyria. And you read two psalms of the Assyrian crisis: Psalm 75, on God’s set time to judge, and Psalm 76, a victory song for Zion. The week taught that God is holy, that he rules history, and that he sends a child who will be the Prince of Peace.
reflectionQuestions: God’s holiness means that he is set apart and morally pure. How does that change the way you think of coming to him?
Isaiah 9:6 gives four names for the coming king. Which of these do you most need Jesus to be for you this week, and why?
The oracles against the nations show that God rules all of history. What situation in the world or your own life is easier to face when you remember this?
prayerPrompts: Thank God for the child born and the son given.
Pray that his government and peace would grow in your life.
Rest in him as Prince of Peace.
